items.name: sqlite
items.description: The fastest cgo-free SQLite driver for Go's database/sql. It builds with CGO_ENABLED=0, and on most workloads it beats the cgo driver too.

readme.excerpt:
It is for Go programs that keep their data in SQLite and want to stay plain Go: one static binary, cross-compiled from any machine, no C compiler in the build or in the container. Until now that meant giving up speed. Here the cgo driver is the one that falls behind.

While building Tifa, I wanted every app to deploy as one Go binary copied to a small VPS. The data had to live in SQLite, and CGO had to stay off, or there goes cross-compiling and the scratch image.

The pure Go drivers paid for that in speed. modernc translates SQLite's C into Go and ncruces runs it as WebAssembly, and both trailed the cgo driver. So I had LLVM compile SQLite's own C straight into Go assembly, and kept at it until the cgo driver was the one falling behind.
features: Writes never wait for the upload. A slow or unreachable store never slows a write or makes it fail. Changes wait on disk next to the databas
Nothing else to deploy. It is a package in your program, so the deploy stays one binary, with no Litestream process beside it.
Every file is checked on restore , then PRAGMA integrity check runs, and a database already there is never written over.
Litestream reads the same copy. It is laid out as Litestream lays it out, and the tests have litestream restore rebuild it at every point an
r.Sync(ctx) waits until what you committed is in the store , for the writes that must be safe before you go on.
No C anywhere. CGO ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build from a Mac works, and the binary runs in a scratch image.
Many writers stop waiting on each other. When goroutines write at the same time, the driver runs their autocommit INSERT , UPDATE and DELETE
Writers queue instead of failing with database is locked . Inside the driver one connection of your program writes a file at a time, and the

items.name: Wireless-Device-Battery-Monitor
items.description: Show the battery level of wireless mice, headsets, keyboards and controllers on the Windows 10/11 taskbar. Lightweight tray app, no vendor software needed. Supports Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, Corsair, HyperX, Glorious, PS4/PS5 DualSense, Xbox and Bluetooth devices.

readme.excerpt:
Formerly Wireless Battery . Version 1.1.0 renamed the app; an update keeps your settings, startup choice and battery history.

Battery levels of your wireless mouse, headset, keyboard and controller, right on the Windows taskbar.

- Tiny : a ~350 KB app using about 2 MB of RAM. It's plain C++/Win32, with no runtime and no background service, and supports per-user installation without administrator rights. - Vendor apps usually aren't required : most drivers query devices directly. Some headsets use the bundled HeadsetControl helper. Device-specific setup, firmware patches and conflicts with vendor apps are described in the table and Limitations. - Many brands : Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, Corsair, HyperX, Glorious, Jabra, JBL, PlayStation and Xbox controllers, Samsung Galaxy Buds, any Bluetooth device Windows knows a battery level for, and every headset the bundled HeadsetControl supports.

items.name: splash
items.description: A local inference engine for Apple silicon, built around the model.

readme.excerpt:
A local inference engine for Apple silicon, built around the model.

Splash runs coding agents and OpenAI or Anthropic compatible applications on one Mac. It combines DFlash 2 speculative decoding, specialized Metal kernels, and automatic memory planning, with vision, tool calling, and a built-in chat page. It reuses cached prefixes and batches concurrent requests automatically.

Download the Splash desktop app for an Apple M3 or newer on macOS 26.4 or later, open the disk image and drag Splash into Applications.

items.name: nsgo
items.description: A cross-platform native UI engine with a Go backend: write apps in Go with signals, memos and flexbox layout, and each platform draws with its own native views — iOS and its App Clips, tvOS, watchOS, macOS, Windows, Android, Linux, the web and WeChat, QQ, Alipay and Douyin mini programs

readme.excerpt:
A cross-platform native UI engine with a Go backend: app logic, the reactive graph and layout run in Go, and each platform draws with its own native UI. It follows the design of Native Shell (NSH) , for teams that want NSH's model without writing Rust.

- Native views. Text, input methods, scrolling, menus and accessibility are each platform's own, and what one platform has, such as Liquid Glass, the others imitate. - Every platform from one Mac. Go builds every target, with Xcode for iOS, tvOS and watchOS and an NDK only for the x86 64 Android emulator: no Android SDK, JDK, GTK or Windows toolchain. - Fine-grained updates. Components run once and signals update only what reads them, with flexbox and grid layout, CSS-like styles, Tailwind classes, themes and animations on the platform's frame clock. - Components. base offers unstyled components from buttons to a million-row DataTable , charts, flow diagrams, a code editor, a rich-text editor and a terminal, and ui gives them NSGo's look. - Platform services. Navigation, notifications, permissions, pickers, sharing, haptics, in-app purchases, widgets and Live Activities, and on desktops windows, panels, menus, tray icons and global shortcuts. - Localized. YAML message catalogs with CLDR plurals, numbers and dates, and right-to-left layout. - TSX apps. Write apps in TSX as NSH does, with hot updates that keep state, and ship them as signed, sandboxed packages a Go app runs. - Tests that act as users do. nsgotest presses, types
